claims.text: The Baltimore Sun of 25 December 1993 reports Testor Corp. selling 'the SR-75 Penetrator and XR-7 Thunderdart, the latest in a series of highly speculative military miniature models', developed by analysing 'sonic boom patterns over Southern California, jet exhaust patterns over Nevada, journals on Stealth and high-speed jet technology, and informed aviation-industry speculation'.
The same article names the designer: 'John Andrews, an aviation historian in San Diego who designed the new models, as well as the F-19.'
The same article carries the Air Force's on-record denial, from Capt. Mary Dillon, an Air Force spokeswoman in Washington: 'We're not saying no comment, we're saying such a plane does not exist.'

claims.source: Reasoning over the Baltimore Sun of 25 December 1993 and slide 62 onward of the 1998 presentation; research/leads/verified-tr3b-2026-09-18.md section 6.3
claims.text: Stated inference. 'SR-75 Penetrator', a mothership carrying a smaller high-speed vehicle, is a specific and unusual concept that was published commercially, in a box, with a designer's name on it, in 1993. Fouche presents the same designation and the same mothership architecture in August 1998 as inside knowledge. Either the kit anticipated a real programme, which is what the audience was invited to conclude from the F-19 precedent the article itself cites, or the account absorbed the kit. Nothing opened decides it. The priority is documented and one-directional and must not be inverted.

desc: This node exists because it is the only documented prior-art channel found for any part of the Fouche account, and because it is documented on both ends. On 25 December 1993 the Baltimore Sun reported that Testor Corp. was selling 'the SR-75 Penetrator and XR-7 Thunderdart, the latest in a series of highly speculative military miniature models', designed by 'John Andrews, an aviation historian in San Diego who designed the new models, as well as the F-19', and said to have been developed by analysing sonic boom patterns over Southern California, jet exhaust patterns over Nevada, published stealth and high-speed literature and industry speculation. The same article carries the Air Force on the record through its spokeswoman Capt. Mary Dillon: 'We're not saying no comment, we're saying such a plane does not exist.' Four and a half years later Fouche's presentation devotes slides 62 onward to an 'SR-75' called the 'Penetrator' that is also 'a mothership', and elsewhere to an 'SR-74 Scramp'. The designation and the mothership architecture are the same, the priority is documented and one-directional, and the direction of influence is not established. The node is here so that a build session cannot accidentally let the TR-3B cluster imply the reverse.
